title: Syncope: Identify Cardiac Risk Before Calling It Vasovagal
bottomLine: Syncope is transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion. The NP priority is to identify cardiac, hemorrhagic, thromboembolic and other dangerous causes before assigning a benign reflex or orthostatic explanation.
recognize: Vasovagal syncope often has a trigger/prodrome and rapid recovery; exertional syncope, abnormal ECG, structural heart disease or family history of sudden death raises cardiac risk.
Older adults may have multifactorial syncope from medications, orthostasis, arrhythmia or structural disease.
differentiate: Seizure usually has a different recovery pattern and may include prolonged postictal confusion; hypoglycemia and intoxication can mimic syncope.
Falls without true loss of consciousness should not automatically be labelled syncope.
assessment: Obtain event/witness history, orthostatic vitals when safe, cardiac and neurologic examination, medication review, bleeding assessment and pregnancy status when relevant.
Ask specifically about exertion, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations and family sudden death.
workup: ECG is core testing; additional rhythm monitoring, CBC, glucose, electrolytes, pregnancy testing or imaging is presentation-driven.
Routine neuroimaging or EEG is low-value in uncomplicated syncope without focal neurologic or seizure features.
management: Urgently evaluate high-risk cardiac, hemorrhagic or thromboembolic features; manage clear reflex/orthostatic causes with trigger, hydration and medication strategies when appropriate.
Unexplained recurrent or high-risk syncope warrants cardiology/rhythm evaluation.
medicationSafety: Antihypertensives, diuretics, nitrates, alpha blockers and QT-prolonging drugs can contribute and should be reviewed rather than reflexively continued unchanged.
redFlags: Family history of sudden unexplained death
counselling: Discuss driving/work restrictions according to cause and current Canadian jurisdictional/CCS guidance rather than a universal interval.
followUp: Close the loop on rhythm monitoring and specialist testing; reassess if the pattern changes.
examTrap: Ordering routine CT head for uncomplicated syncope while missing exertional or ECG red flags.
oneLinePearl: Syncope plus exertion or an abnormal ECG is cardiac until proven otherwise.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society Syncope Clinical Practice Update

title: Pericarditis and Myocarditis: Chest Pain Beyond Coronary Ischemia
bottomLine: Pericarditis and myocarditis can mimic ACS but carry different complications. Diagnose from the whole syndrome—pain pattern, ECG, biomarkers, ventricular function, inflammatory/infectious context—and look first for tamponade, malignant arrhythmia, heart failure or hemodynamic compromise.
recognize: Pericarditis often causes pleuritic/positional chest pain and diffuse inflammatory ECG changes; myocarditis may present with chest pain, troponin elevation, arrhythmia or new ventricular dysfunction after infection or immune exposure.
Myopericarditis/perimyocarditis overlap exists and requires ventricular-function assessment.
differentiate: Regional ischemic changes and a coronary symptom pattern favour ACS; tamponade physiology changes a pericardial effusion from a finding into an emergency.
Troponin elevation alone cannot distinguish myocarditis from MI.
assessment: Assess recent infection, autoimmune disease, medication/immune therapy, pregnancy, hemodynamics, JVP, heart sounds, edema and arrhythmic symptoms.
workup: Use ECG, troponin, inflammatory markers and echocardiography; cardiac MRI or specialty testing is selected according to severity and diagnostic uncertainty.
Do not delay ACS evaluation when ischemia remains plausible.
management: Treat uncomplicated pericarditis according to current evidence and specialist/local pathways; myocarditis with ventricular dysfunction/arrhythmia requires cardiology follow-up and activity restriction.
Tamponade, shock, sustained arrhythmia or severe heart failure requires emergency care.
medicationSafety: NSAID/colchicine use depends on renal/GI/pregnancy context and diagnosis; anticoagulation decisions require caution with significant pericardial disease/bleeding risk.
Avoid strenuous exercise during active myocarditis until specialist clearance.
counselling: Explain activity restriction and why recurrent chest pain after a viral illness still requires reassessment when dyspnea, syncope or palpitations appear.
followUp: Track symptoms, ventricular function, rhythm and inflammatory course; refer persistent/recurrent disease or uncertain etiology.
examTrap: Calling every troponin-positive viral chest-pain syndrome MI—or reassuring a pericardial effusion without checking hemodynamics.
oneLinePearl: Inflammatory chest pain is diagnosed by pattern, but instability is managed before the label.

title: Severe Blood Pressure: Target-Organ Injury Defines the Emergency
bottomLine: Hypertensive emergency is severe blood-pressure elevation with acute target-organ injury. The number alone does not define the emergency; neurologic, cardiac, vascular, renal, retinal or pregnancy-related injury does.
recognize: Concerning presentations include focal deficit, encephalopathy, seizure, pulmonary edema, ischemic chest pain, tearing chest/back pain, acute kidney injury, visual loss and pregnancy/postpartum severe features.
Pain, anxiety, missed medication and measurement error can produce marked BP elevation without acute organ injury.
differentiate: Severe asymptomatic hypertension generally needs confirmation, medication review and timely oral management—not rapid IV normalization.
Pregnancy/postpartum hypertension has syndrome-specific thresholds and drugs and should use the obstetric emergency pathway.
assessment: Repeat BP correctly; assess mental status, focal neurology, cardiopulmonary status, volume/perfusion, pregnancy/postpartum state, stimulant/cocaine exposure and abrupt medication withdrawal.
workup: Tailor ECG/troponin, creatinine/electrolytes, urinalysis, fundoscopy and imaging to suspected organ injury; avoid the same broad panel for every asymptomatic high reading.
management: Emergency organ injury requires ED/hospital management with syndrome-specific controlled BP reduction.
Without acute injury, address triggers, restart/intensify appropriate oral therapy and arrange close follow-up while avoiding precipitous reduction.
medicationSafety: Rapid overcorrection can cause cerebral, coronary or renal hypoperfusion in chronically hypertensive patients.
counselling: Explain the difference between a dangerous number with organ injury and a high reading that still needs prompt but controlled outpatient treatment.
followUp: Severe asymptomatic hypertension needs prompt reassessment and medication/access review.
examTrap: Rapidly normalizing BP solely because the reading is high in an otherwise asymptomatic patient.
oneLinePearl: Treat the organ injury, not panic generated by the number.

title: Cardiac Biomarkers: Injury, Congestion, and Trend in Clinical Context
bottomLine: Cardiac biomarkers answer different questions. High-sensitivity troponin detects myocardial injury and requires serial/ischemic context to diagnose MI; BNP/NT-proBNP supports heart-failure probability/risk but is modified by age, renal function, obesity and AF. Biomarkers never replace the bedside syndrome.
recognize: A rise/fall in troponin supports acute injury but sepsis, PE, myocarditis, tachyarrhythmia and renal disease can elevate troponin without type-1 MI.
BNP/NT-proBNP may rise with ventricular wall stress and support HF diagnosis/risk, but false reassurance/elevation occurs in important contexts.
differentiate: Myocardial injury is not synonymous with myocardial infarction; MI requires ischemic evidence.
CK-MB is generally not preferred when modern troponin testing is available.
assessment: Interpret biomarkers with symptom timing, ECG, hemodynamics, renal function, arrhythmia, PE/sepsis/myocarditis risk and prior values.
workup: Use the local validated high-sensitivity troponin serial algorithm; pair natriuretic peptides with imaging/examination when HF is suspected.
Avoid serial biomarker testing when the result will not change the clinical decision.
management: Treat the clinical syndrome causing myocardial injury or congestion; activate ACS/HF/PE/sepsis/myocarditis pathways according to the evidence rather than the laboratory label alone.
medicationSafety: Do not give antithrombotic ACS therapy merely because troponin is elevated without ischemic evidence; balance bleeding risk and the true diagnosis.
redFlags: Rapid biomarker rise with clinical deterioration
counselling: Explain that an abnormal troponin means heart-muscle injury occurred, but additional evidence determines the cause.
followUp: Ensure abnormal biomarkers are assigned to a diagnosis/workup and not simply copied forward as 'elevated'.
examTrap: Calling every elevated troponin an acute coronary thrombosis or using BNP alone to diagnose heart failure.
oneLinePearl: Troponin tells you injury; the ECG, symptoms and physiology tell you why.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society ACS and heart-failure resources

title: ECG Interpretation: Rate, Rhythm, Axis, Intervals, Morphology, Clinical Risk
bottomLine: Advanced-practice ECG interpretation is systematic and clinical. Confirm technical quality, then assess rate, rhythm, axis, intervals and QRS/ST-T morphology; immediately escalate ischemia, high-grade block, pre-excitation, dangerous QT patterns and unstable wide-complex rhythms rather than chasing every minor automated interpretation.
recognize: ECG interpretation should be reproducible: rhythm/atrial activity, AV conduction, QRS width/morphology, repolarization and comparison with prior tracings.
Automated ECG statements are aids, not diagnoses, and are particularly unreliable for artifacts, paced rhythms and some ischemic/arrhythmic patterns.
differentiate: Sinus tachycardia is a physiologic response until a primary tachyarrhythmia is documented.
Wide-complex tachycardia should be treated as ventricular until appropriately evaluated; ST elevation has ischemic and nonischemic mimics.
assessment: Tie the ECG to symptoms, hemodynamics, electrolyte/drug exposure, prior ECG, structural disease and syncope/family history.
workup: Repeat ECG with correct lead placement when artifact or evolution is possible; use serial ECG/troponin, electrolytes, echo or rhythm monitoring when the clinical question requires it.
management: Escalate ECG evidence of STEMI, unstable tachy/bradyarrhythmia, high-grade block or severe QT/electrolyte risk using the appropriate acute pathway.
Stable incidental abnormalities should trigger cause-directed follow-up rather than reflex emergency treatment.
medicationSafety: Review QT-prolonging and rate-slowing drugs when conduction/repolarization abnormalities appear; correct clinically important electrolyte contributors.
counselling: Explain important ECG findings in relation to symptoms and risk rather than alarming patients with every nonspecific automated phrase.
followUp: Compare with prior tracings and close the loop on rhythm monitoring/cardiology when syncope, inherited risk or unexplained abnormalities persist.
examTrap: Accepting the machine interpretation without checking rhythm, QRS width, ST-T morphology and clinical context.
oneLinePearl: Read the ECG in the same order every time, then ask what finding changes the patient's risk today.

title: Pacemakers and ICDs: Treat Bradycardia, Prevent Sudden Death, Verify the Indication
bottomLine: Pacemakers and ICDs solve different problems. Pacemakers treat clinically important bradyarrhythmia/conduction disease; ICDs terminate life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias or reduce sudden-death risk in selected high-risk patients. Device referral follows symptoms, rhythm/EF phenotype and optimized medical therapy—not the presence of one ECG abnormality.
recognize: Symptomatic high-grade AV block or significant sinus-node dysfunction may require pacing; isolated asymptomatic first-degree or bundle-branch findings often do not.
ICD consideration depends on documented ventricular arrhythmia or persistent sudden-death risk after the applicable disease/medical-therapy assessment.
differentiate: A pacemaker does not provide the same ventricular-tachyarrhythmia protection as an ICD; CRT is a resynchronization therapy for selected ventricular-conduction/HF phenotypes.
Syncope in a patient with conduction disease requires cause assessment rather than automatic reassurance after one normal ECG.
assessment: Assess syncope/presyncope, rhythm documentation, structural heart disease, EF, heart-failure status, reversible causes, life expectancy/goals and medication contributors.
workup: Use ECG/rhythm monitoring and echocardiography as appropriate; reassess LVEF after guideline-directed HFrEF therapy before primary-prevention ICD referral when the CCS pathway calls for it.
management: Refer symptomatic/high-risk conduction disease promptly for pacing assessment and ventricular-arrhythmia/high-risk cardiomyopathy/HFrEF for ICD/CRT assessment according to CCS criteria.
After implantation, ensure device-clinic/remote monitoring and evaluate shocks, syncope and pocket/infection complications.
medicationSafety: Do not use pacing as a substitute for correcting reversible drug/electrolyte causes of bradycardia when safe to do so.
Multiple ICD shocks, ongoing syncope or electrical storm is an emergency.
redFlags: New syncope in a device patient
counselling: Explain the purpose of the device, shock plan, wound/pocket warnings and current CCS/provincial driving restrictions based on diagnosis and events.
followUp: Ensure device interrogation/remote follow-up and reassess underlying HF/arrhythmia therapy rather than treating the implant as the end of care.
examTrap: Referring for an ICD solely because EF was low before adequate HFrEF therapy was established or assuming every conduction abnormality requires a pacemaker.
oneLinePearl: Pacing treats clinically important bradycardia; ICD therapy treats or prevents lethal ventricular rhythm risk.
sourceBasis: CCS Fitness to Drive 2023 rhythm/device guidance
